summary:
Nova – Survival Guide: Martian Map
Project Summary
Imagine you are going on a hike in the mountains. Before leaving, you probably check a map to see where the path goes, how steep the hills are, and what difficulties you might face. Now imagine doing the same thing on Mars. There are no roads, no familiar places, and no one nearby to help if something goes wrong. Astronauts will have to explore an entirely unfamiliar world, so having a good map is not just useful – it could be essential for their survival.
This is where Nova comes in. Our idea is to create a platform that brings different scientific maps and data about Mars together in one place. Instead of searching through many separate sources, users can explore the planet, understand its surface, and plan their journeys more easily.
How Our Project Helps
With Nova, users can explore the Martian surface in 2D and 3D, check the height and steepness of different areas, and see what the terrain looks like. They can choose a starting point and a destination, and our route planner uses the A* algorithm to find possible paths while avoiding dangerous slopes, rough terrain, and reported hazards. It can also suggest alternative routes and a way back.
We also understand that maps cannot show everything. That is why Nova highlights areas where the available information is incomplete instead of promising that every route is safe.
details:
Nova – Survival Guide: Martian Map

Nova is a planetary exploration and route-planning platform designed to support future surface exploration missions, particularly on Mars. Its purpose is to bring together scientific data from different space missions into one interactive environment, allowing users to examine planetary terrain, analyse environmental conditions, and plan possible routes based on real scientific information.

The platform addresses an important challenge of Mars exploration: astronauts and rover operators must navigate unfamiliar terrain without direct assistance from Earth. To support this process, Nova combines multiple scientific datasets, including MOLA, CTX, HiRISE, THEMIS, and Viking data. These sources provide different types and levels of detail, from global elevation models to high-resolution orbital imagery and thermal observations. The system also supports Kaguya elevation data for the Moon and Copernicus GLO-30 for Earth.

Nova provides interactive 2D and 3D maps of Mars, the Moon, Mercury, and Earth, with a Venus preview. Users can switch between available map layers, examine terrain at different resolutions, check elevation and slope at specific coordinates, generate elevation profiles, and visualize local terrain using real digital elevation models (DEMs).

A central component is the Route Planner, which uses the A* pathfinding algorithm to calculate possible paths between selected starting points and destinations. Users can add waypoints and choose between Conservative and Standard terrain profiles. The routing system considers surface slope, roughness, and reported hazards when calculating routes. It can generate a primary route, an alternative route, and an optional return route. Results include distance, elevation gain and loss, slope information, and elevation profiles. Routes can also be visualized directly on 3D terrain.

An important feature is the system's approach to data reliability. Planetary datasets have different resolutions, coverage areas, and levels of accuracy. Nova identifies sections where available elevation data is insufficient and marks unverified route segments with dashed red lines. Each route provides information about its underlying data sources and limitations. The platform does not claim that calculated routes are guaranteed to be safe for astronauts.

Additional functionality includes a hazard reporting system for features such as craters, cliffs, and dunes, with source and verification information. Mission Management allows users to save exploration missions and import or export them as ZIP packages with checksums. Offline functionality supports working without an active internet connection and synchronizing changes later. An optional AI assistant translates natural-language requests into route-planning settings, while the routing algorithm itself remains responsible for calculating paths.

The platform combines geospatial information systems (GIS), DEM processing, terrain analysis, pathfinding algorithms, and 3D visualization. Its architecture is designed to bring together remotely accessed and locally available scientific datasets within a single mapping environment.

Beyond Mars exploration, Nova can support scientific education, planetary research, and terrain-analysis practice on Earth and the Moon. Future development can expand its scientific capabilities through geological points of interest, rover photographs, mission observations, and dedicated scientific stops along exploration routes.

Nova aims to connect planetary scientific data with practical exploration planning, providing a unified environment for understanding unfamiliar worlds and evaluating possible surface journeys.
